newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian economic reformers vow to show who's boss.
newsitem.headline: Russian economic reformers vow to show who's boss.

text.p: A Russian government vow to push through budget cuts despite resistance from parliament is the clearest sign yet of how worried reformers are that their latest economic plans could fizzle out before they even start to work.

First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, whom President Boris Yeltsin charged with leading a new round of free market reforms in March, said on Tuesday the government had done all it could to compromise with the State Duma lower house.
But deputies had proved to be unable to take tough decisions and had preferred to rise for a two-month summer break, he said.

"If the Duma does not take on responsibilities, it makes one doubt whether it is capable of working," he said. "Out of three questions, the Duma completely failed to take a decision on two of them...It suggests the majority in the Duma is not capable of taking political responsibility to the extent demanded today."

The Duma gave initial approval to the government's new tax code last week but on Monday voted down a bill to slash 1997 budget spending. On Tuesday, it rejected the bulk of the government's package of welfare reforms and spending cuts.

"It's being said that if the Duma doesn't cut spending, the government will do so by decree," said Catherine MacDougall, Russia analyst at Kleinwort Benson in London. "The government is not going to be stopped on this one."

The debate between reformers and parliament over the cuts, which could total nearly $20 trillion and affect everything from salaries to funding for industrial enterprises, have become a barometer of just how tough Russia's 100-day-old, fresh-faced cabinet is willing to get.

Having the bills thrown out was no great defeat, emerging markets analysts said -- as long as the tight spending which ministers have vowed to enact, with or without parliament, helped to spur investment and growth.
"Politics aside, the operation of a budget on a real basis is a plus," said one Western economist, referring to the fact ministers were committed to spending less no matter what.
"But even though a lot of the fundamentals are in place, there's broad economic stagnation."

The face of the Russian economy has acquired a new glow in recent months with Russia's hugely successful, third, $2 billion Eurobond, an upbeat assessment at the Group of Seven richest industrialised nations summit and a booming stock market.
The yearly inflation rate, already down to a record low of 14.6 percent in May, is much healthier than the triple-digit levels of a little over a year ago.

The government is gunning for an annual rate of five percent in 1998 and will make the cost of borrowing even cheaper by pushing yields on government securities down to 12 percent from today's 20 percent.
But the economy also has a darker pallor from its struggle to emerge from seven years of severe contraction. The budget deficit is seen as the biggest threat yet to stabilisation.

Gross domestic product (GDP), the broadest measure of economic activity, slipped 0.2 percent in the first five months of this year compared to a year earlier and is forecast to fall two percent in 1997. Portfolio and direct investment are nudging up, but Russian savers still shift dollars out of the country.

Chubais and fellow First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov -- the boy wonders of the new market-minded Russia and the drivers of its reforms -- have said spending cuts, along with reforming natural monopolies and cracking down on tax debtors, are the keys to real growth taking place in 1998.

"The government's going to go ahead with the cuts anyway -- Chubais has said if the money's not there, it can't be spent," said Eastern Europe analyst Charles Robertson. "But there are still some dangers here -- at what point will the population get upset about wage arrears and lose faith in democracy?"
Chubais is a hate-figure for the opposition, which opposes cuts in Soviet-style bottomless-pocket social subsidies.

He and Nemtsov, worried about the effect of perilously low tax revenues on economic and political stability, have moved Russia into new territory by threatening debtors with bankrupty, pushing a corporate-friendly tax code through parliament and persuading privatisation officials to speed up sell-offs.

"It's not a painless process and we're moving in the right direction and rather swiftly," said MacDougall. "But unless things are done swiftly, the economy is not going to grow, and then you can get back to a politically sensitive situation."
